newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania to send troops to join Albania mission.
newsitem.headline: Romania to send troops to join Albania mission.

text.p: Romania's parliament on Wednesday approved the deployment of 400 troops in a multinational military mission to lawless Albania despite opposition attacks that the operation was costly and dangerous.
Parliament voted 231 to 61 with 64 abstentions to send the troops at the request of President Emil Constantinescu. The leftist and nationalist opposition voted against or abstained.
"By acting in Albania, Romania actually defends its own security," Foreign Minister Adrian Severin told a joint session of parliament's two chambers.
"When your neighbour's house is in flames you have to go and help him to prevent the fire engulfing your own yard."

The Romanian contingent of the Italian-led force, made up of 392 infantry men and eight officers, is to be deployed starting next week in the Adriatic ports of Vlore and Sarande and the town of Gjirokaster in rebel-held southern Albania.

Parliament also approved Constantinescu's request to use the airport in the western Romanian city of Timisoara, on the border with Serbia and Hungary, as a logistics and supply base for the Albanian operation.
The government has promoted the operation, estimated to cost the equivalent of $9.5 million as a trump card in its longshot campaign to win early NATO admission.
"This action is in line with our efforts to intergrate in the structures of the Western military alliance," Severin said.
"Romania is, can and must be a regional power," added Emil Tocaci of the National Liberal Party, part of the governing centrist coalition.
Romania, like Albania a Balkan state, hopes to be included alongside favourites Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic when NATO's first wave of expansion is announced in July.
The Albania operation is intended to secure ports and main airports and give the Tirana government time to reorganise the armed forces ahead of elections planned for June.

Albania, Europe's poorest nation, plunged into turmoil when get-rich-quick investment schemes collapsed earlier this year and armed rebels took control of the south during un unchecked spasm of looting and banditry.

During Thursday's debate, nationalists and leftists led by the Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), thrown out of office last November, said money allocated for the operation would be better spent on humanitarian aid.

"We are categorically against any deployment of Romanian troops in Albania which could have serious consequences," said nationalist Valeriu Tabara. "Our troops could engage in clashes with mercenaries supporting (Albanian President Sali) Berisha."
Ruling coalition members jeered in derision at nationalist appeals to keep young Romanian soldiers at home.
"How can you be so careless about those whom you are sending to death?" said Tudor Marcu of the Greater Romania Party. "This is an adventure which could cost many lives."
